newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Markets upbeat as S.Africa brings down fx barriers.
newsitem.headline: Markets upbeat as S.Africa brings down fx barriers.

text.p: South Africa won praise from the markets and the press on Thursday for its latest move to chip away at the walls which have guarded the country's siege economy since the apartheid era.

Long bond yields fell to their lowest levels in 16 months and the Johannesburg Stock Exchange all-share and industrial indices hit new record highs as investors welcomed the government's plan to ease exchange controls on individuals from July 1.
The rand was slightly weaker as South African banks bought dollars in preparation for increased client demand next week.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel announced on Wednesday a higher than expected offshore investment limit for individuals of 200,000 rand ($44,000).

Worries that the move might spark a flight of capital and a run on the rand were soothed by central Reserve Bank predictions that the measure would trigger outflows of only three to five billion rand, which would be roughly matched by inflows.

Underpinning upbeat market sentiment are hopes that a successful relaxation of controls, coming after evidence of a slowdown in the economy, could pave the way for a cut in the country's punitively-high interest rates.

"On the whole there is every reason to be pleased with the foreign exchange limits announced by the finance ministry yesterday," Business Report newspaper said. "The likelihood of haemorrhaging the reserves seems remote."

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals painted an optimistic credit outlook in an interview with state radio on Thursday, saying the lower trend in interbank market rates was "right", although the central bank remained reluctant to lead the way.

A Reuters survey of 31 economists underlined the view that South Africa would weather the latest relaxation of exchange controls without undue damage to official reserves or the rand, setting the scene for an official rate cut around September.

Official reserves were predicted to stand at 22.1 billion rand by the end of August, fractionally up on the 21.8 billion rand at May 31. The rand was seen easing modestly to 4.68 against the U.S. dollar by year-end from 4.51 at present.
The central bank has built up a formidable war-chest to protect the currency from any short-term shocks caused by the latest foreign exchnage moves.

In addition to already record May reserves, bolstered by the sale of 30 percent of Telkom for $1.26 billion, the authorities are also expecting some four billion rand from the government's recent Yankee and samurai bond issues.
Furthermore, the central bank is setting up a $1.5 billion credit facility.
All in all, Stals reckons he has a hefty 38 billion rand at his disposal -- equivalent to nearly four months' import cover.
The markets appear confident that will be enough to cushion any near-term outflows, allow for a one-point rate cut and set the scene for the next set of exchange control relaxations.

Although the July 1 allowance is a milestone for private investors -- effectively lifting 35 years of capital controls for many individuals -- financial institutions and corporates remain severely shackled in the amount of money they can export.
Manuel reiterated on Wednesday the government's commitment to removing all exchange controls as soon as possible.
Business Day newspaper said prompt movement to the next phase was important to keep the markets' confidence in the reform process.
"The danger of a protracted wait is of speculation against the rand that could force the South African hand," it said in an editorial.

($ = 4.505 South African Rand)
